common_name: Crazy Daisy Shasta Daisy (Fringed Spidery Double White Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September-March. Crazy Daisy is grown for its unusual fringed, spidery double flower form rather than the classic simple daisy shape.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Shasta daisies must have excellent drainage and fail in wet, heavy soils. Crazy Daisy bears double, shaggy, spidery white flowers with narrow, twisted petals radiating out in a tangled, fringed mass around the golden central disc, a novelty flower form quite different from the clean, simple daisy shape of classic Shasta cultivars. Its unusual texture makes it a good conversation piece in a mixed perennial border or cutting garden among more traditional daisy-form companions. Like other Shasta daisies it can be a short-lived perennial in hot, humid Gulf South summers; divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and deadhead spent blooms to extend the flowering season.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Leucanthemum Cultivars

common_name: Silver Princess Shasta Daisy (Compact Dwarf White Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September-March. Silver Princess is a compact, dwarf Shasta daisy cultivar suited to the front of a border or small container.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Shasta daisies must have excellent drainage and fail in wet, heavy soils. Silver Princess bears classic single white daisy flowers with golden-yellow central discs on a compact, dwarf plant considerably shorter than standard Shasta daisy cultivars, fitting neatly into a small perennial bed, rock garden, or container where a taller Shasta would overwhelm the space. Like other Shasta daisies it can be a short-lived perennial in hot, humid Gulf South summers; divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and deadhead spent blooms to extend the flowering season.

common_name: Real Neat Shasta Daisy (Compact Fringed Quill-Petaled Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September-March. Real Neat bears unusual narrow, quill-shaped fringed petals on a compact plant.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Shasta daisies must have excellent drainage and fail in wet, heavy soils. Real Neat bears white flowers with narrow, quill-like, slightly fringed petals radiating out from the golden central disc, a fine-textured novelty form on a compact plant that stays tidy without staking. Its unusual, airy flower shape adds textural interest to a mixed perennial border among broader-petaled daisy companions. Like other Shasta daisies it can be a short-lived perennial in hot, humid Gulf South summers; divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and deadhead spent blooms to extend the flowering season.

common_name: Broadway Lights Shasta Daisy (Pale Yellow Aging to White Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September-March. Broadway Lights is grown for its unusual color-changing flowers, opening pale yellow and fading to white as they age.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Shasta daisies must have excellent drainage and fail in wet, heavy soils. Broadway Lights bears flowers that open a soft, pale primrose-yellow and gradually fade to white as they mature, so a single plant often shows both colors at once across different-aged blooms, an unusual color-shifting trait rare among Shasta daisy cultivars, which are almost always solid white. This two-tone effect gives the plant a softer, more layered look in a mixed perennial border than a uniform white Shasta daisy. Like other Shasta daisies it can be a short-lived perennial in hot, humid Gulf South summers; divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring or fall to maintain vigor, and deadhead spent blooms to extend the flowering season.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Leucanthemum Cultivars
